Your team stores Terraform state in an S3 backend with DynamoDB locking. A teammate's"terraform apply failed halfway due to a network issue. Now you see some resources created in AWS, but the next "terraform plan" from your machine shows many of them as new resources to
be created. What is the most appropriate first step to safely reconcile the state with the real infrastructure?
A Manually edit the state file in S3 to add the missing resources and rerun "terraform plan".
B Run 'terraform apply -replace=*' to force Terraform to recreate all resources and refresh state.
C Use 'terraform import' to import the existing resources into the state before running "terraform plan" again.
D Delete the S3 state file so Terraform will create a new one that matches the current infrastructure.
The situation describes drift between the real infrastructure and Terraform state because the previous apply failed mid-run. The correct way to reconcile
existing resources that are not in state is to import them. "terraform import' (or import blocks) associates real resources with Terraform-managed
resources in state, after which "terraform plan" will show accurate changes.
A: Manually editing the state file is strongly discouraged; it is error-prone and not the recommended workflow. B: -replace=* would destroy and
recreate all resources, which is risky and unnecessary; it doesn't reconcile state with existing resources. D: Deleting the state file makes Terraform treat
everything as new, likely causing duplicate resources and loss of history.

You have a saved executionplan containing desired changes for infrastructure managed by
Terraform. After running terraform apply my.tfplan, you receive the error shown.
How can you apply the desired changes? (Pick the 2 correct responses below.)
A. Generate a new execution plan file with terraform plan, and apply the new plan.
B. Run terraform apply without the saved execution plan.
C. Force the apply command by adding the flag -lock=false.
D. Refresh the current state data using the -refresh-only flag.
E. Update the current plan file using the terraform state push command.
A: The plan is stale because state changed after it was created. The correct fix is to recreate the plan
against the latest state and apply that new plan.
B: Running terraform apply without specifying the old plan causes Terraform to re-plan using the
current state and configuration, then apply the resulting changes.
C: -lock=false disables locking; it does not make an old plan valid and is unsafe in team
D: -refresh-only changes what's recorded in state (when applied) but does not "unstale" an existing
E: terraform state push is for advanced/manual state management and does not update a saved plan
file; using it here is inappropriate and risky.
Key Concept: Saved plans are tied to a specific state snapshot; if state changes, you must re-plan.

A. Code contains tabs for indentation instead of spaces
B. There is a missing value for a variable
C. The state file does not match the current infrastructure
The terraform validate command is used to check for syntax errors and internal consistency within
Terraform configurations, such as whether all required arguments are specified. It does not check for

collection of values that are accessed by arbitrary labels, called keys. The keys and values can be of
any type, but the keys must be unique within a map.

useful for grouping related values together, such as configuration options or metadata.
